rationale.campaign_length: The 10 shared missions form a relatively short opening, but further content follows when the mission tree changes.
rationale.colonization: Expansion uses war and formation rather than overseas colonization.
rationale.complexity: Clan support, mask choices, and formation preparation require coordination.
rationale.dark_story: The Facestealer family tragedy and terror raids have clear narrative support.
rationale.difficulty: Unification, raiding, and formation thresholds create difficulty; no in-game sample was performed.
rationale.diplomacy: Clan support and formation conditions affect integration.
rationale.early_pressure: A strong queen and active war create opportunity and contest pressure.
rationale.magic_artifice_intensity: Ancestral masks, shamans, and the Facestealer struggle are the shared core.
rationale.narrative_density: The Faceless Queen event adds a Y91-specific layer to the shared story.
rationale.tall_play: The shared route restores the homeland; Hus Bhal also rebuilds the mountains.
rationale.trade_economy: The route centres on loot and the homeland economy, not trade.
rationale.warfare: The shared route unifies the steppe and raids neighbours.

identity.appearance: A Kuuldaar tribe in 1444, ruled by Nurgai and at war with V25; shared tree and exclusive events.
identity.formation_scope: Conditional formations are Guwaamud Y96, Daxugo Y98, and Baztungh Khayus V28. Y96 and Y98 change technology groups and replace the shared tree with non-generic missions; V28 is not inferred to inherit that tree change.

survey_region.note: Rank 197 aggregate entry; Y91 is a member of the six-country shared-tree compilation, not a predecessor substitution.

national_ideas.scope_note: National traditions, seven ideas, and an ambition; racial and government bonuses are excluded and candidate sets are conditional, not simultaneous.

description.text:
“Strange customs in these lands. They bury their dead like the Yan south of the misty hills instead of giving them a proper sky burial like Tsagaan taught our people. Here they fear not the facestealers. Many of the folk might’ve never encountered one in their lives, ever ignorant of what prowls further north.”

“They stray from Tsagaan’s wisdom.”

“Indeed my little one, they do. They, however, are not to be dismissed as complete fools. The way Tsagaan taught us served a purpose, specifically to combat the facestealing threat. If this threat is no longer present, the ritual can be potentially omitted. We have a lot to learn from the Kuuldaar in all aspects of life. Their art of the bow and its use from atop a terror-bird is a real sight to behold. I am old, but you and your cousins will be taught the way of the bow by our southern kinsmen. Their cultural ties to the Yan can prove useful for our clan, allowing our spies and informants to blend more easily in the south. Get used to these new traditions Nurgai. We may be here for a while”.

description.text:
Nurgai stood in the Tsarai family tent with her two cousins, patiently listening to them discussing the clan’s next moves. It was rather unusual for someone outside the main branch to take part in these private deliberations, but Utalaai considered her more as a sister than a distant cousin. The sole survivour of the Bagaatun family, the former Kaasheg had adopted her in all but name.

“It’s been a decade since we’ve been pushed south by the treacherous scum, if we do not act swiftly we risk our clan being a footnote in the history of the Shuvüüshudi. We must pr-”

“Brother, excuse my interruption.The traitors have the momentum still; they claim legitimacy by donning the mask of the Old, despite being unworthy of even looking at it. If we want to succeed we need to first prove ourselves to the clans, gather them behind our banners. Yanshen is in turmoil and we must make the most out of our unfortunate relocation towards the border.”

After much deliberation, it was decided that revenge had to wait. There was opportunity in the south. The last question that needed to be answered was how to breach the border fortifications protecting the lower Yan.

“Zhiqian”, Nurgai uttered her first word of the evening. “I have a plan.”

description.text:
When the Bhaatum returned from the first Shuvüüsh incursion into Yanshen in ages, the Kaasheg, Utalaai ak-Tsarai, did not return with it. Despite the joy of being successful in raiding all the way to the mouth of the Yan river and the eagerness to sort their loot, the clan had to proclaim a new leader.

The eldest of a well-respected family spoke first. “Utalaai’s children are still very young, leaving his brother, Khaaldak, as the only choice. He has proven himself time and time again.”

No one spoke back, only faint murmuring being heard among the various family heads present at the gathering, until Khaaldak himself stood up, the Tsarai mask firm in his hand. “Your words are wise elder, and I thank you for the nomination. However, there is someone far more deserving of the position. Someone with much more potential than me.”

Everyone knew who he meant. She had captured the fort of Xuanbik and led the Tsarai host all the way to the great city of Tianlou. Be it not for the unfortunate death of the Kaasheg, who knows what other machination she would have devised. No one argued against the proposal. The clan had a Kusheng for the first time, and soon, the entire Shuvüüshudi would follow her lead.

description.text:
“They are on the back foot, the Manticore Banner is flying over less and less Guwaduun settlements. The spirit lovers in the east have them retreating for the steppe.” Nurgai nodded for the faceless informant to continue on.

“The west is also in turmoil. The disparate Kuuldaar clans are all fighting between themselves for dominance, seeking to claim Ulaan’s mask from its shrine. The overseeing Death-Priest has vowed to not allow anyone to enter the shrine until the unnecessary bloodshed of our kin has ceased, however that might come to be.”

“What of the traitors?” The Kusheng’s voice toneless, with no emotion shown whatsoever, yet she was touching a subject most sensitive.

The informant took a few seconds to answer. “The Hus Bhaal have consolidated their control. They are actively sending envoys south, trying to find allies among the Kuuldar. It’s a short matter of time until Ashag Kuulgo also submits to them and the-”. Nurgai gestured to the informant to stop speaking, then stood up, the informant immediately doing the same. She exited the tent after a courtesy bow to the Kusheng. The next morning the bhaatum was mustered, ready to march north.

description.text:
After her unification of the steppe, everyone thought Nurgai would immediately march east and try to emulate Bhengudak’s conquest of the now fractured Dowon splinter states. She, however, knew that the Gowon were well prepared for her. The large mask-wearing Guwaadun population in the east served as the perfect cover for the Tsarai network of informants to operate in.

The armies of the Gowon alliance stayed levied at the border for months waiting for the seemingly inevitable invasion of the newly ascended Queen. Instead, a lone messenger arrived on his terror-bird. When the Shuvüüsh conducted diplomacy, they would arrive mounted on their terror-birds if the message was that of war. The alliance feared the worst, but were slightly relieved when they read the proposal.

“The steppe has been pacified and the Kaashegate has no intention to cross into Gowon. You are relieved of your duty protecting the old Daengun territories in Yanshen, for the Great Kusheng shall take on this mantle. In exchange for delivering you this tranquility, we ask for access to Bhengudak’s great temple and his mask.” It was not so much a proposal as a threat. The Gowon silence was interpreted as a form of silent acceptance.

description.text:
It has been decades since that fateful day. The day she felt she was destined for greatness, her arrow as if guided by the Shepherd themselves. Raising Altan’s mask from the pretender’s lifeless body, she had no desire to wear it. It would be an easy way to cement her legitimacy but Nurgai had vowed to unify the Shuvüüsh by merit and merit alone. She returned the mask to its shrine in Zougzengom, making sure that all could see her never wearing it. She had even refused the Tsarai clan’s mask when she was proclaimed Kusheng, even allowing her cousin to wear it instead, an act of defiance that almost cost her legitimacy in her people’s eyes.

Now she stood here, at the royal palace of Damaogong, having led the Shuvüüsh to what is arguably their greatest achievement. Her wisdom and might considered by all to be unmatched, despite seemingly never having communed with any of the great ancestors. But they were wrong on one account; after unifying the Shuvüüsh, she had secretly travelled to Bhengudak’s temple and briefly wore the mask by revealing her identity to the overseeing Death-Priest.

“Our purpose is to guide the Saanorgegh faithful until the day the masks will be broken and we return to the Supreme Spirit. You, Nurgai, have no need of our guidance. Forge your own legend.”

description.text:
Throughout her reign, Nurgai Bagaatun kept breaking tradition after tradition of Shuvüüsh rulers. Early in her life she had shown fascination with the Luzhong empire’s wonders in the southern steppe, keenly studying the ruins of their once great fortifications, a curiosity quite uncharacteristic. The first major tradition she broke, was it by intended scheming or sheer circumstance and merit, was her ascension to the head of the Tsarai clan in lieu of her cousin. No one reacted. The refusal to wear the Tsarai mask followed and still, no one reacted. Maybe she had greater ambitions, they thought. The greatest act of defiance though, was the refusal to wear Altan’s mask after reclaiming it. No one reacted, maybe she wanted to first wear another great mask, they thought. Then, she refused to wear any of the great masks, much to the surprise of everyone. No one reacted still. It was too late for that; Nurgai had won the steppe, and with it she had won the respect of all her kin.

After her death following her conquests in Yanshen, Nurgai’s soul was bound to the mask she wore her entire lifetime. While she ruled Khaantar and Yan alike, everyone from the smallfolk to the Yomod Rush and even the eunuchs of Yanshen felt close to Nurgai, as if the nation’s ruler was one of them. Maybe it was the mask. The blank, unadorned, bone-white mask, worn by The Faceless Queen.

description.text: We stand at a crossroads. We have revived Bhengudak’s empire, but there is still work to be done. We may have claimed the mantle, but there is still kin of ours, both east and west, that lives outside the great empire’s borders.Some of them even looking down upon us, the Gowon considering us half-bred barbarians and the Khantaar dismissing us as sedentarized and weak. These affronts have to be rectified. All the Shuvüüsh and every last Gowon must come under the empire’s protection, for that is the only way for peace.

description.text: Bhengudak was the one to unify the Shuvüüsh after centuries of loose confederations of clans and tribes wandering the vast steppe. He was the one to bring the three great Izhuun to heel and subjugate the disparate Bhaatum. He was the one to lead them into Dowon and lay claim to the fertile lands in the east. He was the one to reestablish the Great Kaashegate, and it is we that have achieved this noble goal once more. All of that was done through blood and steel, few ever bowed without the need of violence. The battlefield is where we won our empire, and the battlefield seems to be the only place where we can win it back.

description.text: Bhengudak Izhuun Ak-Tsagaan is our prodigal ancestor and the first person to be deemed worthy by the priesthood to have his soul bound to a unique mask along with the Three Brothers of Yore. His legacy is the pride of our noble clan but it is also a curse. Bhengudak’s achievements cast a colossal shadow that our rulers will have to try very hard to escape from, let alone leave their own marks in history. His great mask is the one favoured by the Kaasheg. In a twisted bittersweet way, Bhengudak is still active in the rule of the empire he established, bound by mystic ritual to provide guidance to Guwaamuud until his great mask is shattered and his soul returned to the Supreme Spirit.

description.text:
Our realm stands at a crossroads between civilizations. Civilizations that have little relation to one another, the diametrically different conditions they were forged in driving them further and further away from one another. To the north, the hardy Khudi, living in a harsh climate with few resources to sustain big populations, constantly trying to survive against nature and spirit alike. To the south, the opulent Yan, satisfying their hubris with grand constructions whenever they aren’t toiling under the boot of some tyrant or dying in some pointless war.

Even in our own realm, the rich cities of the Gowon in the east have nothing in common with the moving settlements of the Shuvüüsh. We must make the most out of this inherent diversity, however difficult managing the needs of people so different in nature might be.

description.text: Bhengudak ruled both as Kaasheg and Ambahoron. The Gowon accepted him as their Sage-King, anointed such in Nakeseom by Sado, a fragment of Huszieng the great fox spirit herself, allowing him to enforce his rule and decrees on the Spirit inhabitants of the realm. This syncretism was maintained through a delicate balance that relied on both our religions fundamentally not being at odds with each other cosmologically, despite our death-priests making most spirits nervous with their mere presence. The spirit-lovers, as some of the more radical Saanorgegh faithful called their eastern neighbours, were not only tolerated, but fully accepted and allowed to practice their local religious traditions and customs.

description.text: At Guwaamuud’s height, trade was flowing freely in the eastern sea. From the very far away lands of the Triunics, to the southernmost Halessi corners of Binhrung and Arawkelin, traders could be spotted traversing the Gowon ports, peddling their wares and buying ours to bring back to their distant homelands. The nomadic Shuvüüsh could not be fully controlled at all times, and thus raids into Yanshen were not an uncommon occurrence to say the least, however none of these transgressions were sanctioned by the official government in Onman. Despite this official policy of peace, maritime trade was the preferred method of commerce for all foreigners, save the occasional Rünsukhi peddler or Rukunai delegation crossing the steppe to engage in trade.

description.text: While the old empire succeeded in balancing the Shuvüüsh and the Gowon, they were always wary of their Gowon subjects’ loyalty to the state. These suspicions were not fully unwarranted of course, as the Gowon needed time to accept the terror-bird riders as their rulers. Thus, the old empire’s military was mostly composed of Shuvüüsh warriors, divided in 5 Uvaadum with a very small number of Gowon serving mainly in non-combat roles. Now that our hold over the east has been solidified and the Spirits of these lands have started to accept our rule more eagerly, it is time to also reorganize our military ranks. The populous Gowon should serve mainly as infantry while the Spirits willing to fight can be assigned the role of elite shock troops. While we may lack the ability to field entire spirit armies as the ancient Sage-Kings did, we can still use them, especially in Yanshen, where many times our enemies lack ways to efficiently deal with them.

description.text:
At first, the Yanshen saw us only as Shuvüüsh invaders, while we called ourselves Daxugo—the Great Empire, believing we were destined to restore order. As we learned their language and script and governed their towns, the Yanshen gradually accepted that Daxugo had taken root in their land. With the signing of the Tianlou Concord between ourselves and the Yanshen states—standing together against external foes and growing ever more intertwined—we ceased to be clearly distinguished from one another: you within us, and us within you.

Yet our ancestral beliefs and customs endured, so that even as we came to be regarded as Yanshen, we retained a distinct character of our own. Over generations, a new identity emerged:

We are Yanshen, and we are the Empire.

description.text:
The soul-farms of the Northern Plains were once regarded as lands where spirits settled more firmly than men. Through the stewardship of successive monarchs and the adoption of Yanshen techniques, these lands have been transformed into fertile fields. Their steady abundance of grain has rooted the people to the soil, replacing wandering with permanence and allowing communities to flourish in stability.

Along the Yanhe, authority restored order; refugees returned in great numbers, merchants gathered once more, and revived river trade bound the region together as towns prospered again.

One land feeds the people, the other gathers them — farmland and markets reinforcing one another, driving Daxugo’s population to unprecedented heights and swelling its armies as never before.

Under our rule, this land has truly become a Land of the Many.

Along the Yanhe, authority restored order; refugees returned in great numbers, merchants gathered once more, and revived river trade bound the region together as towns prospered again.

One land feeds the people, the other gathers them — farmland and markets reinforcing one another, driving Daxugo’s population to unprecedented heights and swelling its armies as never before.

Under our rule, this land has truly become a Land of the Many.

description.text:
As Daxugo’s ties with Yanshen grew ever closer, its military entered a period of transition. The Shuvüüsh elite — the Imperial Spears — upheld the traditional terror-bird shock cavalry doctrine, while the emerging Yanshen Corps advocated integrating terror-birds into disciplined infantry formations.

The clash of these military doctrines reflected the tensions of cultural fusion and gradually reshaped the army. The Imperial Spears began experimenting with applying Yanshen systems of discipline and the use of artillery to terror-bird units, while supporters of Yanshen corps theory increasingly incorporated the terror-birds’ devastating flanking charges into large-scale formations. At the same time, they sought to exploit the terror-birds’ formidable carrying capacity to establish reliable supply lines. Through mutual exchange and adaptation, both sides absorbed the strengths of the other’s doctrine, forging a new path between steppe ferocity and Yanshen order.

description.text:
When our tribes first entered Yanshen, the Faceless Queen was compelled to incorporate the eunuchs into the imperial administration in order to stabilize the realm and ease the burdens of governance. Yet as their influence steadily expanded and they began to encroach upon royal authority, restraining their power became the enduring objective of successive monarchs. Several emperors sought to curb the eunuchs’ dominance—some by elevating decorated Daxugo nobles to court positions as a counterweight, others by establishing a new corps of officials selected independently of the eunuch system to assume their responsibilities. These efforts were not without bloodshed, and palace purges were far from rare.

After a long era of reform, as key state institutions gradually came under the control of the nobility and Daxugo officials chosen through the examination system, the eunuchs were stripped of most of their political authority and redirected toward scholarship, record-keeping, and the arts. With the continued advance of imperial centralization, their influence steadily waned.

description.text:
In the Empire’s early days, when Daxugo had only just transformed from tribes into a monarchy, it struggled to control its distant frontiers. Though Yanshen eunuchs were brought into the administration, the monarch refused to entrust them with full authority. Instead, remote regions were granted to cadet royals or cooperative warlords, giving them the right to raise troops, levy taxes, and maintain their own officials. In return, they were to guard the borders, send regular tribute, and answer imperial calls to war.

Over time, however, these fanwang lords built their own power bases. Some delayed tribute, ignored summons, or forged quiet ties with foreign powers. Far from the capital and commanding their own armies, they shifted from frontier shields to potential threats.

Rumors of conspiracy reached the capital, forcing the monarch to ask:

Should these border realms be entrusted to more reliable hands?

description.text:
Daxugo’s state rites blend the ancient Shuvüüsh mask tradition with the ceremonial order of Yanshen. After fasting, the emperor ascends the altar wearing an unadorned white mask, signifying that he stands beyond any single clan as the ritual bearer of the empire’s shared order, offering sacrifice to Heaven.

The High Priest dons the black mask of the Shepherd of Souls and, amid music and the threefold offering, calls upon the ancestral spirits of the Three Brothers—Tsagaan, Ulaan, and Altan—to watch over the rite; the masks of other honored ancestors are arranged beside him as witnesses to the ceremony.

Terror-birds, revered as sacred beasts and symbols of virtue, take part in the ceremony and lead the ritual procession; their hatchlings are bestowed upon meritorious servants according to Yanshen court tradition.

Through this union of steppe mask-law and Yanshen ceremonial order, Daxugo establishes a unified state rite across its vast domains, affirming its rightful rule and its duty to safeguard all lives within its realm.

description.text:
As Daxugo developed and the surrounding situation evolved, the Empire gradually formed a distinctive diplomatic corps. Unlike settled states that relied on permanent embassies, Daxugo stood between the steppe and the prosperous cities of Yanshen; facing diverse states and circumstances, its envoys evolved into a mobile, composite diplomatic force combining ritualized contractual practices, negotiation, and liaison functions.

These itinerant missions moved between courts, tribal encampments, and commercial cities, handling treaty communication and mediating border frictions. Their experience, forged amid conflicts among the steppe tribes, allowed them to buffer disputes before tensions among concord members escalated, ensuring the continued operation of the defense-oriented Tianlou Concord. By linking networks of relations and trade across the steppe and Yanshen, they also provided concord members with tangible benefits beyond security, exerting lasting influence within the concord framework.

description.text:
Khaantar is a desert wasteland that knows little of mercy, but it is not without boons if one knows where to look. A cave that holds respite; a small river giving bountiful water and pasture; even the very ruins themselves can house a small army in the shade, if needed. Yet there is more to these ruins than just the things needed to live.

Indeed, there are relics within that we can use to thrive. We send parties across these ruins to strip them bare, and to bring them back for study, whether for personal use or for other pursuits such as adorning the rooms of the greatest of us. Some of the Runsukhi and Rukunai have an inkling of what such relics might be used for, and thus are routinely conscripted for these efforts.

The desert houses secrets that the greatest of the Khaantari, the greatest of us, will use to truly thrive in what once was.

description.text:
A mask was a shield to us, a symbol of our heritage and a way to honor our ancestors who have discovered the secrets to ward off the Facestealers. But now that we have achieved so much more than them, is it really so appropriate to wear the mask of just a faceless person, or of these ancestors?

Our masks have grown since our days of warlordship. Now we have become Baztungh Khayus; we have outgrown our need to be a copy, faceless in a crowd, easily forgotten upon death or upon being consumed by Facestealers. Now we can truly express ourselves in a way that represents the core being of ourselves. Gold to go with triumph, red to match honor – a blue fractal pattern to represent endless wisdom. We have grown to wear a new persona for ourselves, and there will be no need to go back to how we were.

description.text:
Glimpse a single terrorbird rider, and know that there are far more on all sides ready to slip in and gut you. You are already dead - they will have set up days beforehand, half a day’s distance to the left of you and to the right – if possible, even half a day behind you. They will wait and wait and wait until the signal is given, just as the eggs of the terrorbirds themselves wait for the right conditions to hatch.

The terrorbird riders are terrifying to behold, the Yomod Rush having perfected the breeding of them to ensure their speed, survivability and intelligence in all conditions under the guidance of a rider. Though there have been some grumblings about the demands of expanding the breeding programs, they still abide by our rule and foresight. Just enough to ensure mass destruction, just enough to ensure the tactics used work as intended.

These are the tactics that evolved from the simple days of warlordism, back when the Baztungh Khayus was just a simple band. Now? Now they ride, and when they ride they leave nothing behind.

description.text:
Those who boast no ancestry in ancient Khaantar are fit only to be tributaries, outsiders with claim to only a fraction of the greatness and protection of the Shuvuushi and Kuuldar.

There is a more fraternal affection of sorts to those that do share that Khaantari heritage. The Runsukhi and Rukunai, those who either stayed within the wastes that once made home or retreated to the plateaus up high, are ultimately our brothers. Some might claim hold truer to Khaantari wisdom than the Shuuvushi, that they should guide the brethren – in this they are mistaken. It was the Shuuvushi and Kuuldar who united all of us, after all. Where our brothers only fought to survive, we fought to thrive. Therefore, it is we who will guide them to greatness, who will stamp down on foolish practices and help them don the masks which protect and represent… whether they want us to or not.

Still, they are treated better than the outsiders, still higher on the hierarchy than them. However, if an outsider were to prove themselves, then perhaps they too might be said to have the blood of Khaantar in their veins?

description.text:
The greatest challenge for a conquering army is information control: that which one gains for oneself, and that which one’s enemy gains. Scouts, watch-towers, and spies are the bane of any army that has to march through hostile lands to reach the fight; traps and poisons are set, lands are burned, any possible means taken to delay progress and cause losses of manpower and material.

But what if you were fast enough? What if you targeted areas where scouts would naturally be placed, to run them down before they could bring back information? What if you quietly suborned the watchtowers? Ensured that no news, no information ever reached the enemy armies, save a terrifying swell of silence? Then, indeed, the enemies would never know you were there, or at least not your true numbers, until it was too late. They would never see it coming.

description.text:
Khaantar was not perfect. They fell, after all, to the teeming hordes of Facestealers and the fall of the land around them. Yet can we truly consider them culpable? How can one truly prepare, truly survive such conditions without splintering, without cracking?

We have the answer. Our ways, perfected over millennia of war. Our roots, torn and adrift amongst the terror birds. Our strength, bound by the rule of our great leaders. Our bonds through kin, our masks, our everything. We have brought order back to Khaantar. And Khaantar shall return, not as the empire that died through ruin, but as an empire that thrives in even the toughest conditions. Decrees shall be made: Khaantar shall be mapped out, with the Runsukhi giving over the finest pastures for the greatest of us. No longer shall we be purely settled; we shall be as we were, true Shuvvushi warlords. No longer will the Rukunai hoard secrets: all will be spilled like entrails from a beast. No longer shall there be any dissent: they will understand that only we can truly guide Khaantar’s beating heart back into place.

This innocent sin will be rectified.

description.text:
Beneath the ruins, nestled into the foot of the four peaks, lies a staff of gleaming purple imbued with powerful spiritual energy. The area is bereft of Facestealers, of horrors, of spirits. It is obvious to us after using it upon a roving Facestealer that it dispels them back wherever they once arose out of; we watch them briefly glow with energy before disappearing utterly.

We shall find where they live, where their cavern of origin lies. We shall use this relic on them, and we shall tear the Facestealers asunder. We will end it thus!
